title: MATH GAOKAO - 414
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.concept: Square proportional relationship in a physical model
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a physical quantity changes when a variable in a square-proportional model is scaled.
questions.question: In a braking-distance model, the distance \(d\) (in meters) is proportional to the square of the speed \(v\) (in meters per second), so \(d=kv^2\) for a positive constant \(k\). If the speed is doubled, what happens to the braking distance?
questions.explanation:
Let the original braking distance be \(d_1=kv^2\). If the speed is doubled, the new speed is \(2v\), so the new distance is
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_2&=k(2v)^2 \\
&=k\cdot 4v^2 \\
&=4kv^2 \\
&=4d_1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the braking distance becomes \(4\) times as large. Option B would correspond to direct proportionality, not square proportionality.
questions.hint: Substitute \(2v\) into the model and compare the result with the original expression.

questions.concept: SI units of a constant in a physical formula
questions.learningObjective: Determine the SI base units of a constant by dimensional consistency.
questions.question: In Newton's law of gravitation \(F=G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}\), where \(F\) is force in newtons, \(m_1,m_2\) are masses in kilograms, and \(r\) is distance in meters, which expression gives the SI base units of \(G\)?
questions.explanation:
Since \(1\,\text{N}=1\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}\), solving the formula for \(G\) gives
\[
G=\frac{Fr^2}{m_1m_2}.
\]
Substituting units,
\[
\begin{aligned}
[G]&=\frac{(\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2})(\text{m}^2)}{\text{kg}^2} \\
&=\text{m}^3\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore option B is correct. Option A is missing the time unit and one power of meter.
questions.hint: Write the unit of force in SI base units and solve the formula for \(G\) before substituting units.

questions.concept: Interpretation of the slope in a linear model
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the rate parameter in a linear physical model.
questions.question: The volume \(V\) of water in a tank, in liters, after \(t\) minutes is modeled by \(V=120-4t\). What does the number \(4\) represent in this model?

options.label: A
options.text: The rate at which the volume decreases, in liters per minute

options.label: B
options.text: The initial volume of water in the tank, in liters

questions.explanation: In the linear model \(V=120-4t\), the coefficient of \(t\) is the rate of change of \(V\) with respect to \(t\). Since \(V\) is in liters and \(t\) is in minutes, the term \(-4t\) means the volume decreases by \(4\) liters per minute. The initial volume is \(120\) liters, not \(4\).
questions.hint: Compare the linear form \(V=b+mt\) with the given equation and identify which number multiplies \(t\).

questions.learningObjective: Determine the unit of acceleration from dimensional consistency in a kinematic model.
questions.question: In the kinematic model \(s=ut+\frac{1}{2} at^2\), \(s\) is displacement in meters, \(u\) is initial velocity in meters per second, and \(t\) is time in seconds. What is the SI unit of \(a\)?
questions.explanation:
The term \(\frac{1}{2} at^2\) must have the same unit as \(s\), namely meters. Since \(t^2\) has unit \(\text{s}^2\), the unit of \(a\) must be
\[
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}=\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}.
\]
Option A is a velocity unit, not an acceleration unit.
questions.hint: Every term in a physically meaningful sum must have the same unit; set the unit of \(at^2\) equal to the unit of \(s\).

questions.concept: Square-root scaling in a physical model
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a quantity changes when a variable under a square root is scaled.
questions.question: The period \(T\) of a simple pendulum is modeled by \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\), where \(L\) is the length and \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity. If the length \(L\) is made \(4\) times as large while \(g\) remains constant, what happens to \(T\)?
questions.explanation:
Let the original period be
\[
T_1=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}.
\]
If the length becomes \(4L\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_2&=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{4L}{g}} \\
&=2\pi\cdot 2\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \\
&=2T_1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So the period doubles, not quadruples.
questions.hint: Compare the new and original expressions for the period while keeping the gravitational acceleration fixed.

questions.concept: Integral of power as total energy
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the definite integral of a power function in a physical context.
questions.question: A device's power output \(P(t)\) is measured in watts as a function of time \(t\) in seconds. What physical quantity does \(\int_{0}^{T} P(t)\,dt\) represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The average power output over the interval \(0\le t\le T\)

options.label: B
options.text: The total energy delivered by the device from \(t=0\) to \(t=T\)

questions.explanation:
Power is the rate of energy transfer, \(P=\frac{dE}{dt}\). Therefore integrating power with respect to time gives total energy:
\[
E=\int_{0}^{T} P(t)\,dt.
\]
The unit is \(\text{W}\cdot \text{s}=\text{J}\), which is energy. Average power would instead be \(\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T} P(t)\,dt\).
questions.hint: Recall the relationship between power, energy, and time, and what operation reverses a rate.

questions.concept: Derivative as a marginal physical quantity
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the derivative of a cost function as a marginal rate in a model.
questions.question: Let \(C(x)\) be the cost, in yuan, of producing \(x\) items. The model gives \(C'(x)=5\text{ yuan}\) per item when \(x=100\). What is the best physical interpretation of this value?

options.label: A
options.text: The additional cost to produce one more item when \(100\) items are already being produced is approximately \(5\text{ yuan}\).

options.label: B
options.text: The total cost of producing \(100\) items is \(5\text{ yuan}\).

questions.explanation: \(C'(x)\) is the instantaneous rate of change of cost with respect to the number of items. At \(x=100\), \(C'(100)=5\) means that increasing production by one item from \(100\) changes the cost by about \(5\text{ yuan}\). It is not the total cost; the total cost at \(100\) items is \(C(100)\), not \(C'(100)\).
questions.hint: Interpret a derivative as a rate of change per unit increase of the input variable.

questions.concept: Unit conversion factor in a model
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a constant used to convert between physical units.
questions.question: A model converts speed \(u\) in meters per second to speed \(v\) in kilometers per hour using \(v=3.6u\). What does the factor \(3.6\) represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of kilometers per hour corresponding to \(1\) meter per second

options.label: B
options.text: The number of meters per second corresponding to \(1\) kilometer per hour

questions.explanation: Since \(1\,\text{m/s}=3.6\,\text{km/h}\), multiplying a speed in \(\text{m/s}\) by \(3.6\) gives the equivalent speed in \(\text{km/h}\). Thus \(3.6\) is the number of kilometers per hour corresponding to \(1\) meter per second. The reciprocal \(\frac{1}{3.6}\) would convert kilometers per hour to meters per second.
questions.hint: Write the equality between \(1\,\text{m/s}\) and \(\text{km/h}\) and see which unit the multiplication produces.

questions.concept: Units of an exponent parameter in exponential decay
questions.learningObjective: Determine the unit of a rate constant from dimensional consistency in an exponential model.
questions.question: A cooling model is \(T(t)=T_0 e^{-kt}\), where \(T\) and \(T_0\) are temperature differences relative to a fixed ambient temperature, measured in degrees Celsius, and \(t\) is time in minutes. What must be the unit of the constant \(k\)?
questions.explanation: In the expression \(e^{-kt}\), the exponent \(-kt\) must be dimensionless. Since \(t\) has unit minutes, \(k\) must have unit \(\text{min}^{-1}\). Temperature units do not enter the exponent because \(T\) and \(T_0\) appear outside the exponential factor.
questions.hint: An exponent of an exponential function cannot carry a physical unit; it must be dimensionless.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the unit of a coefficient by requiring dimensional consistency in a physical law.
questions.question: Newton's law of cooling is modeled by \(Q=kA(T-T_0)\), where \(Q\) is heat loss rate in watts, \(A\) is surface area in square meters, and \(T-T_0\) is temperature difference in kelvins. What is the SI unit of \(k\)?
questions.explanation:
Solve the equation for \(k\):
\[
k=\frac{Q}{A(T-T_0)}.
\]
Substituting the units, \(Q\) is in watts, \(A\) is in \(\text{m}^2\), and \(T-T_0\) is in \(\text{K}\). Therefore
\[
[k]=\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}\,\text{K}^{-1}.
\]
Option A uses joules, which is energy, not power; it is missing the per-second aspect of watts.
questions.hint: Write the equation as \(k=\frac{Q}{A(T-T_0)}\) and substitute the units of each quantity.
